subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A step-up transformer:
questions.explain: A step-up transformer increases the voltage and decreases the current (power is conserved).

questions.q: How can the magnetic field of an electromagnet be made stronger?
questions.explain: Adding an iron core (or increasing current/turns) increases the strength of an electromagnet.

questions.q: Electromagnetic induction is the production of:
options: A magnetic field by a current
A potential difference when a conductor and magnetic field move relative to each other
questions.explain: A voltage is induced when there is relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field.

questions.q: In a simple generator, a larger induced voltage can be produced by:
questions.explain: Rotating the coil faster increases the rate of change of the field, increasing the induced voltage.

questions.q: Why does the National Grid transmit electricity at very high voltage?
options: To make the electricity travel faster
To reduce the current and so reduce energy lost as heat in the cables
To increase the current in the cables
questions.explain: High voltage means low current, which greatly reduces energy wasted as heat in the transmission lines.

questions.q: How could you reverse the direction of the force on a wire in an electric motor?
options: Reverse the direction of the current
questions.explain: Reversing the current (or the magnetic field) reverses the direction of the force.

questions.q: A permanent magnet is one that:
options: Produces its own magnetic field all the time
Only becomes magnetic when near another magnet
questions.explain: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field continuously.

questions.q: A plotting compass can be used to:
options: Show the direction of a magnetic field
questions.explain: A plotting compass needle lines up with the field, showing its direction.

questions.q: An induced magnet is a material that:
options: Becomes magnetic only when placed in a magnetic field
questions.explain: An induced magnet becomes a magnet only when it is placed in a magnetic field.

questions.q: Which material would make the BEST permanent magnet?
questions.explain: Steel is magnetically hard and retains its magnetism, making good permanent magnets. Soft iron is easily magnetised but loses it quickly (good for electromagnet cores), while copper and aluminium are non-magnetic.

questions.q: Fleming's left-hand rule is used to find the direction of the:
options: Force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field
questions.explain: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force in the motor effect.

questions.q: An advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet is that:
options: It can be switched on and off
questions.explain: An electromagnet can be turned on and off by controlling the current.

questions.q: Two magnets are placed near each other. Which pairing will REPEL?
options: A magnet near an unmagnetised iron nail
questions.explain: Like poles repel, so two north poles push apart. Unlike poles (N–S) attract, and an unmagnetised iron nail is always attracted (induced magnetism).

questions.q: A compass needle always points roughly north. What does this tell us?
options: Compasses are attracted to the Sun
Magnetic fields do not affect compasses
The Earth has a magnetic field, evidence its core is magnetic
The Earth has no magnetic field
questions.explain: A compass needle is a tiny magnet that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, providing evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.

questions.q: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet point:
options: From south pole to north pole outside the magnet
From north pole to south pole outside the magnet
Into the magnet at both ends
questions.explain: By convention, field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.

questions.q: An alternator produces:
questions.explain: An alternator uses slip rings to produce an alternating current.

questions.q: When a current flows through a straight wire, it produces:
options: A magnetic field in circles around the wire
questions.explain: A current-carrying wire creates a circular magnetic field around it.

questions.q: A solenoid is:
options: A coil of wire that produces a magnetic field like a bar magnet when carrying current
A permanent magnet made of plastic
questions.explain: A solenoid is a coil of wire whose field, when carrying current, resembles that of a bar magnet.

questions.q: A transformer only works with:
questions.explain: Transformers require a changing (alternating) current to induce a voltage in the secondary coil.

questions.q: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet STRONGEST?
options: At the poles, where the field lines are closest together
At the centre of the magnet
Where the field lines are most spread out
Everywhere the field strength is the same
questions.explain: The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field. Lines are most concentrated at the poles, so the field is strongest there.

questions.q: The force between an induced magnet and the magnet that induces it is always:
questions.explain: Induced magnetism always produces a force of attraction towards the inducing magnet.

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the first finger represents the:
questions.explain: The First finger points along the magnetic Field, the seCond is Current and the thuMb is Motion (force).
